steps: Check the fireplace
Code-complying masonry fireplace only, never factory built. Minimum opening 25 3/4" W x 23 1/2" H x 12.5" D. Plan non-combustible floor protection: 16" (USA) / 18" (Canada) in front, 8" each side.
Consult the authority having jurisdiction (building or fire department) before installation about the need for a permit (p. 1).
Plan the 6" liner

Continuous 6" liner from the appliance to the top of the chimney, to Class 3 of CAN/ULC-S635 or CAN/ULC-S640. Recommended minimum 15 ft vertical, stove top to termination, at 0–1000 ft; more with altitude or elbows (p. 12).
Inspect & prepare the chimney

Have the masonry chimney inspected by a certified professional to NFPA minimums and cleaned: no cracks, loose mortar, deterioration or blockage. If the fireplace is modified, fix the supplied metal tag where it stays visible.

Attach the tag with screws or nails where it is readily visible if the insert is removed. It reads: "This fireplace has been altered to accommodate a fireplace insert and should be inspected by a qualified person prior to re-use as a conventional fireplace."
Fit the shroud side panels

Unpack the unit and set it in front of the opening (don't slide it in yet). Slide the left and right shroud side panels onto the 4 protruding screws on the back of the firebox, drop them into the key hole notches (Fig. 1), then fully tighten the screws.
Level the insert

Thread the supplied leveling bolts into the four 3/8" NC nuts at the rear corners and below each front grille. It must sit level and slightly higher than the protruding hearth front; shim only with non-combustible material such as firebricks.
Slide it in
Slide the unit into the fireplace opening. On a rough hearth, set the 2 supplied metal strips under the leveling bolts so it slides.
Connect the liner

Working through the opening above the unit, attach the flue liner and appliance connector to the flue collar. If access is too tight, remove a shroud side panel, or slide the unit back out to make the connection.
Fasten all vent joints with sheet metal screws and run a bead of furnace cement around the flue collar connection (p. 11).
Upper shroud & thermometer

Slide the upper shroud panel down so the tabs on its back go over the receiving flange on top of the appliance, then fasten it to both side panels (Fig. 2). Fit the catalytic thermometer into the hole in the appliance top.
Convection deck & trim

Center the convection deck on top and fasten it to the upper shroud panel with 2 screws (long drive bit needed, Fig. 3). If purchased, fit the shroud trim kit: corner brackets into the top piece, then the side pieces, fastened at the bottom.
Hang the loading door
Seat the bottom door hinge hole on the bottom hinge pin, then the top; lower until the hinge surfaces meet (Fig. 4). The door is heavy. Never operate with the door off or left open.

Satin or gold plated doors: follow the "Plated door and trim care" card in the manual kit. Then complete the installer details on the last page of the manual (p. 44) and leave the manual with the homeowner (p. 1).

panels.title: Not enough heat
items: Green or wet wood → check it with a moisture meter
Not enough fuel → load fully; a full load burns no hotter than the thermostat is set
Combustor plugged, coated or not working → clean or test it; replace if needed
Thermostat set too low → raise the setting
Poor draft or downdraft → measure draft with a manometer; wind-resistant chimney cap
Tight house or too few coals → open a window slightly or add an outside air kit; build a larger coal bed

panels.title: Too much heat
items: Bypass door left open → close it
Thermostat set too high → lower the setting
Leaking loading-door gasket → replace the gasket and/or adjust the door
Excessive chimney draft → measure with a manometer; install a cap
Wood too small → use larger pieces
Thermostat not working properly → consult the dealer

panels.title: Smoke spills when loading
items: Spark arrestor screen plugged → clean it to bare metal wire
Chimney too cold → use double wall stove pipe
Not enough vertical rise → at least 36" before elbows; two 45° elbows instead of one 90°
Chimney not drafting → thermostat to highest, bypass open, loading door closed, wait 5-10 minutes

panels.title: Thermometer won't reach Active
items: Improper operation → check the thermostat setting and operating procedure
Obstruction in chimney or cap → clean the chimney
Faulty catalytic thermometer → check its calibration
Wood too green or wet → use seasoned wood
Combustor plugged or not working → clean, test, replace if needed
Bypass door leaking or not closing → clean around it; adjust or replace the gasket

light.title: Starting a fire
light.html:
Light it by hand with paper and kindling, right on the firebricks at the bottom of the firebox. Never use a grate.

  1. Check that all the firebricks are in place.
  2. Turn the thermostat to High. Turn the fan off, if you have one.
  3. Open the bypass, then open the loading door.
  4. Put 10 balls of non-glossy paper near the front. Crisscross 20 pieces of kindling on top, leaving air gaps.
  5. Light it and leave the door cracked open. Stay with the fire.
  6. Once the kindling is fully burning, add two or three medium logs. Keep the door unlatched until they catch.
  7. Latch the door. When the combustor temperature starts to climb, close the bypass.
  8. When nearly all the wood is burning and the needle is in the active zone, open the bypass and door, load as far back as you can, then latch the door and close the bypass.
  9. Leave it on High until the fire is well established and the needle is in the active zone (at least 500F).
  10. Then gradually turn it down to the heat you want.
Leaving the door open once the wood has caught may make the combustor fail early.
Note: the manual's step 7 says to turn the fan on to high once the door is latched and the combustor starts to climb; its step 11 says to turn the fan on after the initial warm up (p. 20); the fan section says to keep it off until the stove reaches normal operating temperature (p. 16).

controls.title: Thermostat, bypass & thermometer
controls.html:
Thermostat knob

It's on the right side of the insert. At High the fire burns fastest and gives the most heat. Turning the knob clockwise lowers the burn rate and the heat. Make changes gradually; a fast change can make the thermostat work poorly. It's set at the factory, so don't tamper with it.

Turned down too low or too quickly, the fire can go out or the combustor can stop working. Just turn it back up and let the fire re-establish. The tested low-burn position is shown as a picture on p. 22.

Bypass handle

It's on the right side of the front. Lift it up to open the bypass when you light or reload; push it down to close it. A bypass left open is a listed cause of too much heat.

Catalytic thermometer

It sits on top and shows whether the combustor is active or inactive. Inactive means the combustor is below 500F and not burning clean, so keep the needle in the active zone.

Fan (if equipped)

About 30 minutes after the fire is established, match the fan speed to the thermostat: low with low, medium with medium, high with high.

Note: p. 18 says to turn the fan off for about 5 minutes before you read the thermometer; p. 29 and p. 35 say 10 minutes.

reload.title: Reloading the fire
reload.html:
Check the catalytic thermometer first. If the needle is still in the active zone, use the steps below. If it has dropped into the inactive zone, start again with the lighting steps.

  1. Have the next load of wood ready. Turn the thermostat to High and wait a few minutes.
  2. Open the bypass and wait a few more minutes. This cuts down smoke spilling into the room.
  3. Crack the loading door open and give it about a minute to settle.
  4. Open the door slowly and load. If smoke spills out, close the door a little until the draft picks up.
  5. Latch the door and close the bypass right away. Leave it on High until the fire is well established, then turn it down.

Don't be afraid to fill it: the wood only burns at the rate the thermostat is set. Load only within the shaded area pictured on p. 19; loading beyond it voids the warranty.

Glass getting dark? Long, very low burns leave creosote on the glass. Run on High for about 30 minutes to burn most of it off.
The insert is hot. Keep children and pets from touching it, and keep anything that can burn at least 48" from the front. Don't store wood in the clearance space or where you stand to reload or remove ash.

wood.title: Choosing firewood
wood.html:
Burn natural cord wood only. Aim for a moisture content of 20% or lower: use wood that has been split, stacked so air reaches it, and kept out of rain and snow for at least 24 months. Wet wood wastes heat and greatly increases creosote. Air-dried, seasoned wood lowers the risk of chimney fires and gives higher efficiency and lower emissions.

Hardwood and softwood both burn well. Dense hardwood burns a little slower and longer.

Check it with a moisture meter

  1. Pick three logs at random from the pile and split each one down the middle.
  2. On the split face, measure 2" from each end and in the middle, with the pins in line with the grain.
  3. Average all the readings. It's an approximate guide.

Never burn

  • Wet, green or unseasoned wood. It can cause excessive creosote buildup, and if the creosote ignites, it can cause a chimney fire that may result in a house fire and serious bodily harm.
  • Salt-water driftwood. It corrodes the insert and voids the warranty.
  • Treated or painted wood, coal, charcoal, colored paper, cardboard, garbage or solvents. Burning these may release toxic fumes and/or carbon monoxide, which may result in poisoning.
  • Flammable fluids such as gasoline, naphtha or engine gel.
  • Lots of offcuts, pressed logs or small, very dry pieces as your main fuel. They can overheat and damage the firebox and combustor.
No starter fluids. Never use chemicals or fluids such as gasoline-type lantern fuel, kerosene or charcoal lighter fluid to start or freshen up a fire. Doing so may lead to over-firing, resulting in a house fire and serious bodily harm.

normal.title: That smell, sound or smoke is probably normal
normal.html:
First fires: a strong smell and some smoke

The paint cures the first time you heat the insert and gives off a strong odor with smoke. Burn at a low setting for several hours and open a door or window until it clears. The paint may change color as it cures; it evens out after a few more fires.

Ticks and creaks

Minor expansion, contraction and movement of parts, and the noise that comes with it, is normal (p. 41).

Not much flame on low

On low settings you may not see much flame. If the thermometer stays in the active zone, the burn is still going.

The combustor gets hotter after you turn it down

Turning the thermostat down makes the fire give off more smoke, which fuels the combustor, so its temperature can climb for up to several hours. That's normal (p. 36).

What comes out of the chimney

From a properly working catalytic stove, it's mostly water vapor. In extremely cold weather it can freeze in some outside chimneys; burn on High for 5 to 10 minutes to melt any ice (p. 22).

Smoke when you open the door on a mild day? The chimney draws less in spring and fall. Run on High for 30 minutes after lighting or reloading, and build smaller, hotter fires rather than turning the thermostat way down (p. 22).

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
The best way to keep the glass clean is to burn on a high setting for a while after each reload. That drives off the moisture that leaves creosote on the glass. Before you turn it down for an overnight burn, leave it higher for 30 minutes to an hour.

Cleaning by hand

  1. Wait until the insert and the glass are cool. Never clean hot glass.
  2. Use a soft cloth. No abrasive cleaners.
  3. After any cleaner, rinse the glass well with water. Leftover cleaner bakes on and is very hard to remove.
Be gentle with the glass. Don't strike it or slam the door, and don't use the insert if the glass or its gasket is broken. The warranty covers only heat breakage, not glass that was struck, cleaned with harsh or abrasive cleaners, or hit by wood as the door closed (p. 41).

Check the door seal

With the insert cool, latch the door on a piece of paper, like a dollar bill, and pull it out. You should feel resistance. Repeat all around the door. If there's none, the door tension needs adjusting (p. 31).

ash.title: Removing ashes
ash.html:
Take ashes out whenever they come within one inch of the door opening. Don't remove all of them: wood burns best on a bed of ashes about 1/2" thick.

  1. Make sure the fire is out and the insert is cool to the touch.
  2. Put the ashes in a metal container with a tight-fitting lid. Don't put any other waste in it.
  3. Set the closed container on a non-combustible floor or on the ground outside, well away from anything that can burn.
  4. If you bury or scatter the ashes, keep them in the closed container until all the cinders have fully cooled.
Never store hot ashes in a garage or basement. Hot ashes give off carbon monoxide and flammable gases that can suffocate and kill.
Vacuuming? Only once the fire is out and the insert is cool. Hot ash in a vacuum bag can melt the vacuum and start a house fire (p. 24).

After the last fire of the season, remove all the ash and check inside for warped plates or cracking. Any problem must be corrected before next season, or the warranty is void (p. 16).

combustor.title: Caring for the catalytic combustor
combustor.html:
A combustor that isn't working costs you heat and raises emissions and creosote. A healthy one keeps the thermometer above 500F (active zone) and often runs past 1000 F.

Keep an eye on it

  • Look at it at least three times each heating season for damage. Only take it out if performance drops.
  • Compare the chimney smoke with the bypass closed and open. There should be much less with it closed.

Quick test

  1. Light a fire as usual and let it burn well for 1 hour.
  2. Turn the thermostat to medium-low. After 5 minutes the needle should be in the active zone.
  3. Repeat over at least 3 burn cycles. Still inactive? Clean the combustor. If that doesn't help, it may need replacing: call your dealer. The thermometer itself could also be off.

Cleaning

Only when the fire is out and the insert is cool. Lift off the flame shield, then brush the face lightly with a soft paint brush or pass a vacuum wand near it. No hard tools or pipe cleaners, and leave the combustor in place. A hot fire is usually the best cleaner.

Never run the insert without the combustor or the flame shield. Replacement is best left to your dealer or installer.

The rating label lists the combustor by its OEM part number, 115-Z0444 (p. 4). Blaze King's own part number for the supplied combustor is S.CAT29, which the parts list calls the combustor assembly (p. 26, p. 37).

chimney.title: Chimney care & chimney fires
chimney.html:
Have the chimney and the insert cleaned at least once a year, or as often as needed; a professional chimney sweep is recommended. Check the flue regularly through the heating season, especially the coldest months, until you know how often it needs cleaning. Open the bypass before sweeping so soot falls into the firebox.

Creosote forms when wood burns slowly. The hotter the fire, the less creosote builds up.

If a chimney fire starts

  1. Turn the thermostat to its lowest setting. Make sure the loading door and bypass door are tightly closed.
  2. Call the fire department.
  3. Check the chimney, attic and roof for anything hot enough to catch fire. If needed, use a fire extinguisher or a garden hose.
  4. Don't use the insert again until a certified chimney sweep has inspected the chimney and flue connector.
Note: p. 18 says turning the knob clockwise lowers the burn rate, but p. 33 says to close the thermostat in a chimney fire by turning the knob fully counter clockwise; p. 34 says to turn it to the lowest setting.
Be ready: keep at least one smoke detector and one carbon monoxide monitor in the room with the insert, and a fire extinguisher in a central spot everyone knows (p. 5). Chimney fire damage isn't covered by the warranty.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Blaze King's limited warranty is for the original purchaser, from the date of purchase, on stoves bought from an authorized dealer and installed in the United States or Canada. It can't be transferred.

Catalytic combustor6 years: no charge for the first 3 years, then you pay 60%, 70% and 80% of the retail price in years 4, 5 and 6
Stove body, steel firebox parts5 years: from year 2 you pay a share of the cost, 20%, 40%, 60% and 80% in years 2 to 5
Fans, thermostat, door handle steel parts2 years, parts and limited labor
All parts and materials, incl. paint1 year, parts and limited labor

Making a claim

Report the problem to your Blaze King dealer within 30 days of noticing it, with proof and date of purchase; the dealer makes the claim in writing. A failed combustor goes back to the dealer with a combustor failure report and your original proof of purchase.

Not covered

  • Gaskets and firebrick; normal paint discoloration
  • Over-firing (warped plates, burnt-off paint), misuse, neglect or improper installation
  • Glass breakage other than from heat
  • Damage from salt-saturated, drift or treated wood, or from a chimney fire
  • Removing and reinstalling the stove
Mail in the warranty registration card and have your installer fill in the last page of the manual.

specFlue.title: Chimney liner & venting
specFlue.html:
Flue collar6" I.D. (152.4 mm)
LinerContinuous 6" diameter, appliance to top of chimney
Liner standard (p. 10)Class 3 of CAN/ULC-S635 or CAN/ULC-S640
Liner listing (label, p. 4)6" stainless steel, UL 1777, ULCS635 or ULCS640
Masonry flue area (recommended)no less than 28in² (180cm²)

Blaze King recommends a stainless liner, preferably insulated. Fasten every vent joint with sheet metal screws and run a bead of furnace cement around the flue collar connection (p. 11). Keep an effective vapor barrier where the chimney penetrates the exterior. Never connect to a chimney serving another appliance (voids the warranty). The chimney must extend at least three feet above the roof penetration and two feet higher than any part of the building within ten feet. In tight homes a fresh air intake into the room is recommended.

Note: the rating label says do not remove bricks or mortar in the masonry fireplace (p. 4), but p. 11 allows removing masonry or steel, including the damper plate, from the smoke shelf and adjacent damper frame to fit the liner, provided it doesn't weaken the structure or reduce protection for combustibles below the National Building Code.

conflicts.issue: Which way closes the thermostat in a chimney fire: p. 18 says rotating the knob clockwise decreases the burn rate; p. 33 says close the thermostat by rotating the knob fully counter clockwise; p. 34 says turn it to the lowest setting.
How long the fan must be off before reading the catalytic thermometer: approximately 5 minutes (p. 18) vs 10 minutes (p. 29 maintenance, p. 35 troubleshooting).

When to turn the fan on while lighting: step 7 says turn fan(s) on to high once the door is latched and combustor temperature begins to climb; step 11 says turn it on after the initial warm up (both p. 20); the fan section says keep it off until the stove reaches normal operating temperatures and match the thermostat about 30 minutes after the fire is established (p. 16).

Combustor part number: the rating label gives combustor OEM part number 115-Z0444 (p. 4); the combustor warranty section says the supplied combustor is OEM part # S.CAT29 (p. 26) and the parts list gives S.CAT29 Combustor Assembly (p. 37).
conflicts.reason: Two numbering systems: the rating label gives the combustor's OEM part number, 115-Z0444 (p. 4); S.CAT29 is the OEM Blaze King part number for the supplied combustor (p. 26), listed in the parts list as the combustor assembly (p. 37). The guide shows both and says what each is.

conflicts.issue: Masonry removal: the rating label says do not remove bricks or mortar in masonry fireplace (p. 4); the chimney section allows removing masonry or steel, including the damper plate, from the smoke shelf and adjacent damper frame to accommodate a liner (p. 11). Possibly complementary, but worded as a contradiction.

review.notes: One combined Operation & Installation Manual (180-PI29 v3.01, Feb 14 2025). Not transcribed because they exist only as figures: appliance dimensions with the 29" and 33" shrouds (pp. 7-8); the clearance drawing, including an unexplained 18" (REF) dimension (pp. 4, 9); the usable firebox loading area (p. 19); the tested low-burn thermostat position (p. 22); and the warranty check-mark grid (p. 39). The warranty drawer uses the prose terms on pp. 40-42 instead. The manual prints no efficiency percentage (only that it is HHV per B415.1-10, p. 16), no burn time and no heating area, so the catalog's 79.7% efficiency, 29 hr maximum burn time and 1,000-2,300 sq ft could not be checked. The catalog weight of 325 lb matches the manual's shipping weight (p. 6). The manual treats the fan as optional ('if equipped', pp. 13, 16, 29), matching the catalog's blower field. Troubleshooting says to check draft with a manometer against manufacturer specifications (pp. 28, 34-36), but no draft value is given anywhere. The maintenance list mentions an ash drawer (p. 29); no other page describes one for the PI29. Initial-setup numbering repeats step 5 (pp. 13-14), and reload steps 2 and 3 both say to open the bypass (p. 21); the guide follows the manual's order. Bilingual label text (p. 4) duplicates the English; nothing was French-only, there is no gas-smell block (wood unit) and no font-offset text was found. Owner text writes the knob and thermometer labels (HIGH, ACTIVE/INACTIVE) in normal case.
